title: Music Theory
intro: Music theory explains why music sounds the way it does: how pitches relate, how rhythm is organised, how chords move and how whole pieces are built. It is taught here at the piano, where every pitch has its own key and the patterns of scales and chords are easy to see. The Guitar Theory pages (#/arts/guitar/guitar-theory) apply the same ideas to the fretboard. This topic starts from the physics of a vibrating string and works up through intervals, scales, chords and harmony to counterpoint, form, jazz harmony, tuning and post-tonal music. Every page has sound examples you can play, worked examples and practice problems.

blocks.text: The chapters are in learning order: each one uses the ones before it. If you already read music, skim the first two chapters and start at Intervals. If you play by ear, the first chapter's sound examples and the keyboard widget will connect what you hear to names on the page.

items: Sound and Pitch (#/arts/music-theory/sound-and-pitch): frequency, loudness, timbre, the harmonic series, and how pitch is written down.
Rhythm and Meter (#/arts/music-theory/rhythm): note values, time signatures, syncopation, tuplets and polyrhythm.
Intervals (#/arts/music-theory/intervals): naming the distance between two notes, inversion, and why some intervals sound smooth and others rough.
Scales and Keys (#/arts/music-theory/scales-and-keys): the major and minor scales, key signatures, the circle of fifths, the modes and other scales.
Chords (#/arts/music-theory/chords): triads, seventh chords, inversions, figured bass, extended and altered chords.
Harmony (#/arts/music-theory/harmony): Roman numerals and harmonic function, cadences, voice leading, non-chord tones, secondary dominants, modulation and chromatic chords.
Counterpoint (#/arts/music-theory/counterpoint): combining independent melodies, from first species to free counterpoint.
Form (#/arts/music-theory/form): motive, phrase, period and sentence; binary, ternary, rondo and sonata form; blues and song forms.
Jazz Harmony (#/arts/music-theory/jazz-harmony): chord symbols, the ii–V–I, chord-scale theory and reharmonisation.
Tuning and Temperament (#/arts/music-theory/tuning): just intonation, the Pythagorean comma, meantone and well temperaments, equal temperament and other divisions of the octave.
Post-Tonal Theory (#/arts/music-theory/post-tonal): pitch-class sets, set classes and twelve-tone rows.

blocks.text: The keyboard lays every pitch out in a line, left to right from low to high, with the black keys grouped in twos and threes so you can always find your place. Intervals are distances you can count, scales are patterns you can see, and a chord is a shape under one hand. Most theory teaching uses the keyboard for that reason, and every page here has a keyboard you can play. Where it helps, pages end with an 'At the piano' section: fingerings, hand positions and voicings.

items: Pitch names use scientific pitch notation: middle C is C4, the A above it is A4 = 440 Hz, and the octave number goes up at each C.
♯ (sharp) raises a note by a semitone, ♭ (flat) lowers it, ♮ (natural) cancels either. Double sharps and flats are written 𝄪 and 𝄫.
Roman numerals name chords by the scale degree of their root: upper case for major (I, IV, V), lower case for minor (ii, iii, vi), ° for diminished and + for augmented.
Intervals are measured in semitones (the smallest step on a piano) or in cents, where 100 cents is an equal-tempered semitone and 1200 cents is an octave.

blocks.text: The sound examples use a small piano keyboard widget: click any key to hear it, or press ▶ on an example. The first press may need a moment while your browser starts its audio.
